title: Which Fabric Workload Runs This Job?
purpose: Route a data or analytics job to the right Fabric workload — Data Factory, Data Engineering, Warehouse, SQL Database, Eventhouse, or Power BI — based on what the job actually needs, and show why the choice matters less than it seems because every workload lands data as Delta in the same OneLake.
accessibleSummary: A decision tree that starts by asking what kind of workload a job is: streaming events, batch/ELT ingestion and transformation, or interactive analytics and reporting. Streaming routes to Eventhouse via Real-Time Intelligence. Batch/ELT branches again on engine preference into Data Factory pipelines, Spark notebooks in Data Engineering, or SQL-first Warehouse/SQL Database. Interactive analytics routes to Power BI. All branches converge on OneLake, because every workload persists its tabular data as Delta Parquet there regardless of which engine wrote it, so the choice is about engine fit and skills, not data lock-in. A warning node flags picking a workload by team habit instead of the job's actual shape.
longDescription: This is a decision tree, not a pipeline: it asks what a job needs and answers with a workload, not a sequence of steps that runs in order. The root question separates jobs into three shapes: continuously arriving events, scheduled batch movement and transformation, and interactive human consumption. The streaming branch goes to Real-Time Intelligence's Eventhouse. The batch branch splits again by engine preference: Data Factory pipelines for orchestration-heavy, connector-driven movement across many source types; Data Engineering (Spark notebooks and job definitions) for complex or iterative transformation logic; and Warehouse or SQL Database for teams working primarily in T-SQL, including full multi-table transactions. The interactive branch goes to Power BI, which reads whatever any of the upstream workloads produced. Every branch converges on OneLake, because Fabric persists all tabular workload output as Delta Parquet regardless of the writing engine — the one-copy design that lets T-SQL, Spark, and Analysis Services all read the same physical data without duplication. A workspace-type gate applies underneath all of this: only Fabric, Trial, or P-SKU capacity-backed workspaces can run non-Power-BI-item workloads at all. The warning node calls out the common anti-pattern of choosing a workload from team familiarity rather than the job's actual requirements.

nodes.label: What shape is the job?
nodes.summary: Root question: is this continuous streaming, scheduled batch movement, or interactive consumption?
nodes.detail: The first split is not about which product a team likes — it is about the temporal shape of the job. Continuously arriving events need a different engine than a scheduled batch load, and both differ from a human opening a report. Fabric organizes its functionality into role-oriented workloads that all run in the same environment and can share data without duplication, so this question is about fit, not about being locked into a silo.
nodes.whyItMatters: Answering this first prevents the common failure of defaulting to whichever workload the team already knows, then bending a streaming or transactional requirement to fit a batch tool that was never built for it.

evidence.note: Fabric organizes its functionality into role-oriented workloads — Power BI, Data Factory, Data Engineering, Data Science, Data Warehouse, Databases, Real-Time Intelligence — which all run in the same environment and can share data and items without duplication.

inputs: A stated business requirement (e.g. 'alert on device telemetry', 'load yesterday's orders', 'let analysts self-serve a dashboard')
processing: Classify the requirement's temporal shape: continuous events, scheduled batch, or on-demand interactive query
Check whether the job genuinely needs sub-second reaction, or batch-window freshness is acceptable
outputs: A routed job shape that determines which workload branch to evaluate next
drill.example: A team building a factory-floor anomaly alert routes to streaming; the same team's nightly ERP extract routes to batch, even though both eventually land in the same OneLake tenant.
controls: Write down the actual freshness requirement before picking a workload, not after
failureModes: Defaulting to the workload the team already knows regardless of job shape — see the warning node

nodes.label: Real-Time Intelligence → Eventhouse
nodes.summary: Continuously arriving events route to Eventhouse via Real-Time Intelligence.
nodes.detail: Real-Time Intelligence storage is hierarchical: a workspace can hold multiple eventhouses, each eventhouse multiple KQL databases, and each KQL database multiple tables — purpose-built for high-velocity event ingestion and query rather than scheduled batch loads.
nodes.whyItMatters: Streaming jobs need an engine designed for continuous, high-velocity write and near-real-time query; forcing that shape through a batch pipeline means either polling too slowly or paying for a scheduler that was never built for continuous ingestion.

evidence.note: Real-Time Intelligence storage is hierarchical: a workspace can contain multiple eventhouses, an eventhouse can contain multiple KQL databases, and each KQL database can contain multiple tables.

inputs: Continuously arriving event streams (telemetry, logs, IoT, application events)
processing: Ingest via Eventstream into an Eventhouse KQL database
Query with KQL for near-real-time exploration
outputs: Queryable event tables, plus optional Real-Time Hub discovery for downstream reaction
drill.example: Vehicle telemetry streams into an Eventhouse KQL database, queried within seconds of arrival for a fleet-health dashboard.
controls: Retention policy per KQL database table
failureModes: Routing high-velocity streams through a batch pipeline instead, introducing polling latency the business didn't ask for

nodes.label: Batch/ELT: which engine fits the team?
nodes.summary: Second question for batch jobs: orchestration-heavy movement, Spark transformation, or T-SQL?
nodes.detail: Once a job is confirmed as batch or scheduled ELT rather than streaming, the next question is which engine and skill set should own it: connector-driven orchestration across many source types, Spark for complex or iterative transformation logic, or T-SQL for teams that think in relational terms and need multi-table transactions.
nodes.whyItMatters: This decision is about engine fit and team skills, not about data being locked into one store — all three downstream choices write Delta into the same OneLake, so switching later is a re-platforming choice, not a data-migration one.

inputs: The transformation complexity and the team's dominant skill set
processing: Assess whether the job is mostly connector orchestration, complex procedural transformation, or relational T-SQL logic
Check whether multi-table ACID transactions are a hard requirement
outputs: A routed engine choice: Data Factory, Data Engineering, or Warehouse/SQL Database
drill.example: A job pulling from Snowflake, Databricks, and Salesforce via built-in connectors and merging results routes to Data Factory; a job doing iterative ML feature engineering routes to Spark notebooks instead.
controls: Record the reason for the engine choice so it can be revisited if the job's shape changes
failureModes: Splitting one logical pipeline across engines for team-politics reasons rather than a real technical requirement

nodes.label: Data Factory pipelines
nodes.summary: Connector-driven orchestration across many source types, with logic-heavy workflow control.
nodes.detail: Fabric Data Factory provides built-in connectors and activities for sources like Snowflake, Databricks, Google BigQuery, and Salesforce, and its orchestration engine supports logic-heavy workflow control through If-Condition, Until, and ForEach iterators — a differentiator for complex cross-system workflows that need scheduling, event triggers, and branching control flow rather than raw transformation power.
nodes.whyItMatters: When the job's complexity is in coordinating many systems and triggers rather than in the transformation logic itself, Data Factory's connector breadth and control-flow constructs solve the actual problem instead of forcing that orchestration into notebook code.

evidence.note: Fabric Data Factory provides built-in connectors and activities for Snowflake, Databricks, Google BigQuery, and Salesforce, including notebook/jar trigger activities for Databricks and SFTP-paired movement for Salesforce; its orchestration engine supports logic-heavy workflow control via If-Condition, Until, and ForEach iterators.

inputs: Source connections across multiple cloud platforms
processing: Chain Copy Activities, notebook triggers, and control-flow iterators into a pipeline
Trigger on schedule or on an event such as a new file landing in a lakehouse
outputs: Orchestrated, logged pipeline runs landing data as Delta in OneLake
drill.example: One pipeline extracts from BigQuery, triggers a Databricks notebook to process it, then merges the result into a Snowflake table — all under one pipeline and scheduler.
controls: Retry and error-handling branches per activity
failureModes: Building complex procedural transformation logic inside pipeline expressions instead of handing it to Spark, producing an unmaintainable pipeline

nodes.label: Data Engineering (Spark notebooks)
nodes.summary: Spark notebooks and job definitions for complex or iterative transformation logic.
nodes.detail: Procedural PySpark notebooks are well suited to genuinely complex logic — API ingestion, streaming workloads, ML inference, iterative algorithms, and deeply nested data structures — where declarative SQL expressions would be insufficient or unnatural. Fabric's newer Materialized Lake Views offer a declarative alternative for stable, SQL-expressible logic, but notebooks remain the route for logic that doesn't fit that shape.
nodes.whyItMatters: Forcing genuinely complex procedural logic into a declarative or connector-based tool produces brittle workarounds; Spark notebooks are the workload actually designed for that complexity.

evidence.note: Procedural PySpark notebooks are well suited to genuinely complex logic — API ingestion, streaming workloads, ML inference, iterative algorithms, and deeply nested data structures — where declarative SQL expressions would be insufficient or unnatural.

inputs: Bronze or raw data requiring complex transformation logic
processing: Write PySpark or Spark SQL in a notebook or Spark job definition
Run against a starter or custom Spark pool
outputs: Transformed Delta tables in a lakehouse, immediately queryable by other engines
drill.example: A notebook applies an iterative deduplication and feature-engineering pipeline too complex for declarative SQL, writing conformed Delta tables back to the lakehouse.
controls: Choice between notebook (interactive) and Spark job definition (scheduled, unattended)
failureModes: Using Spark for simple, stable SQL logic that a declarative tool like Materialized Lake Views or dbt would maintain with far less operational overhead

nodes.label: Warehouse / SQL Database (T-SQL)
nodes.summary: T-SQL-first engines with full multi-table transactions, for relational teams and OLTP needs.
nodes.detail: A SQL analytics endpoint provides T-SQL querying over lakehouses, mirrored databases, and SQL databases, while the warehouse item supplies full transactional T-SQL like a traditional enterprise data warehouse, including multi-table ACID transactions. SQL Database in Fabric adds an OLTP-oriented option for transactional application workloads that also need analytics access.
nodes.whyItMatters: When a team's skill base is T-SQL, or a workload genuinely needs multi-table transactional semantics, routing to Warehouse or SQL Database uses the engine actually built for that surface instead of bolting relational logic onto Spark.

evidence.note: A SQL analytics endpoint provides T-SQL querying over items that are not warehouses themselves — available for lakehouses, mirrored databases, and SQL databases — while the warehouse item supplies full transactional T-SQL like a traditional enterprise data warehouse.

inputs: Relational data needing full T-SQL semantics
A requirement for multi-table transactions or OLTP-style writes
processing: Load via COPY INTO, pipelines, or cross-database T-SQL
Execute multi-table transactions where a load must commit or roll back as one unit
outputs: Governed relational tables, physically stored as Delta and published to OneLake
drill.example: A finance team migrating stored procedures loads a warehouse via nightly COPY INTO batches wrapped in a multi-table transaction so a mid-load failure never leaves a partially-updated star schema visible to reports.
controls: Choice between Warehouse (analytics-first, writable T-SQL) and SQL Database (OLTP-first, transactional application backend)
failureModes: Choosing Warehouse for a workload that never actually needs a multi-table transaction, gaining none of its differentiator

nodes.label: Power BI (interactive consumption)
nodes.summary: Interactive analytics and reporting reads from whatever upstream workload produced the data.
nodes.detail: Power BI is one of Fabric's role-oriented workloads and consumes data produced by any of the others through a semantic model, without requiring a separate export or copy step, because all workloads persist tabular data as Delta in the same OneLake.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because Power BI reads the same Delta tables any other workload wrote, an organization doesn't need a separate BI-specific extract pipeline — the canonical pattern is ingest, process, then visualize, with no manual integration step between them.

evidence.note: A canonical end-to-end pattern in Fabric is to ingest data with Data Factory, process it with Data Engineering or Real-Time Intelligence, and visualize the result in Power BI — with no manual service integration because all stages share OneLake and the same platform services.

inputs: A semantic model over Delta tables produced by any upstream Fabric workload
processing: Build measures and relationships in a semantic model
Publish reports and apps for consumption
outputs: Interactive reports and dashboards for business consumption
drill.example: A semantic model reads gold Delta tables a Spark pipeline wrote overnight, with no export step between the two workloads.
controls: Semantic model storage mode (Direct Lake, Import, DirectQuery)
Row-level security defined on the model
failureModes: Building a bespoke export pipeline into Power BI when Direct Lake could read the Delta tables directly with no refresh

nodes.label: OneLake (shared Delta store)
nodes.summary: Every workload's output lands as Delta Parquet in the same tenant-wide OneLake.
nodes.detail: All Fabric data items, including lakehouses and warehouses, automatically persist their tabular data in OneLake using the open Delta Parquet format, regardless of which engine wrote the data. This one-copy design lets multiple Fabric engines — T-SQL, Apache Spark, Analysis Services, and others — operate over the same physical data without duplicating datasets per engine.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is why the workload choice earlier in the tree is lower-stakes than it looks: picking Data Factory over Spark, or Warehouse over SQL Database, does not lock data into a silo, because every path converges on the same open Delta store the other engines can still read.

evidence.note: All Fabric data items, including lakehouses and warehouses, automatically persist their tabular data in OneLake using the open Delta Parquet format, regardless of which engine wrote the data; the one-copy design lets multiple engines operate over the same physical data without duplication.

inputs: Delta tables written by Data Factory-orchestrated jobs, Spark notebooks, Warehouse loads, or SQL Database replication
processing: No conversion — every engine already writes Delta natively
Metadata registers the table so any other engine can read it immediately
outputs: A single tenant-wide OneLake namespace queryable by T-SQL, Spark, KQL, and Analysis Services alike
drill.example: A Warehouse table loaded via T-SQL and a lakehouse table written by a Spark notebook sit side by side in OneLake, both readable by the same downstream semantic model.
controls: Workspace and capacity placement (governs region and billing, not data format)
failureModes: Standing up separate physical data stores per team out of habit, recreating the duplication OneLake is designed to eliminate

nodes.label: Trap: routing by habit, not job shape
nodes.summary: Picking a workload from team familiarity instead of the job's actual requirement produces a poor fit.
nodes.detail: A team fluent in Spark can technically force a streaming or transactional job through notebooks, and a T-SQL-first team can force complex iterative logic into stored procedures, but both choices fight the workload instead of using the engine built for the job's actual shape. The workspace-type gate compounds this: only Fabric, Trial, or P-SKU capacity-backed workspaces support running non-Power-BI-item workloads at all, and a Premium Per User license cannot substitute for a capacity to create items like lakehouses or warehouses.
nodes.whyItMatters: Routing by habit rather than requirement is the most common way a Fabric implementation ends up with the wrong engine under a workload years into its life, at which point migrating is a re-platforming project rather than a one-time decision.

evidence.note: Relying on Power BI Premium Per User (PPU) licenses to run Fabric workloads is a mistake: PPU is a per-user feature set, not a capacity, so it cannot create or run non-Power BI Fabric items such as lakehouses, warehouses, or notebooks — an F or Trial capacity is still required.

inputs: A job whose actual shape doesn't match the team's default workload
processing: Force-fit the job into the familiar workload anyway
Discover the workspace's capacity type doesn't even support the item being created
outputs: A brittle implementation that fights its own platform, or an outright blocked item-creation attempt
drill.example: A T-SQL-only team builds an iterative feature-engineering job as nested stored procedures instead of a Spark notebook, hitting complexity limits a notebook would have handled natively; separately, a team on a Pro/PPU-only workspace discovers they cannot create a lakehouse without an F or Trial capacity.
controls: Confirm the workspace's capacity type supports the target item type before designing the job
Re-evaluate workload choice against job shape, not team comfort, at design time
failureModes: Multi-year technical debt from an engine mismatch discovered only when the job's complexity or scale outgrows the wrong-fit tool
Blocked deployments from assuming a Pro/PPU license substitutes for a Fabric capacity

edges.label: risk: chosen by habit, not fit

walkthrough.title: 1. Start with the job's shape, not a favorite tool
walkthrough.explanation: Classify the job as streaming, batch/ELT, or interactive before naming a workload — this question determines everything downstream.

walkthrough.title: 2. Streaming goes to Eventhouse
walkthrough.explanation: Continuously arriving events route to Real-Time Intelligence's Eventhouse, purpose-built for high-velocity ingestion and near-real-time KQL query.

walkthrough.title: 3. Batch jobs branch again by engine fit
walkthrough.explanation: For batch/ELT jobs, the next question is orchestration breadth, transformation complexity, or T-SQL/transactional needs.

walkthrough.title: 4. Orchestration-heavy movement: Data Factory
walkthrough.explanation: Connector breadth and control-flow constructs make Data Factory the fit for coordinating many source systems on a schedule or trigger.

walkthrough.title: 5. Complex transformation: Spark notebooks
walkthrough.explanation: Genuinely complex or iterative logic belongs in Data Engineering's Spark notebooks, not forced into declarative or connector tools.

walkthrough.title: 6. Relational/transactional: Warehouse or SQL Database
walkthrough.explanation: T-SQL-first teams and workloads needing multi-table ACID transactions route to Warehouse or SQL Database.

walkthrough.title: 7. Warning: don't route by habit
walkthrough.explanation: Forcing a job into a familiar workload instead of the one built for its shape produces brittle implementations and, on the wrong capacity type, outright blocked deployments.

walkthrough.title: 8. Every path converges on OneLake
walkthrough.explanation: All three batch engines, and Eventhouse alongside them, persist data as Delta in the same tenant-wide OneLake — so the workload choice is about engine fit, not data lock-in.

walkthrough.title: 9. Power BI reads whatever landed
walkthrough.explanation: Interactive consumption reads from OneLake through a semantic model regardless of which upstream workload produced the data, closing the canonical ingest-process-visualize pattern.
